html:
The continuous production week, or nepreryvka, was a Soviet work calendar introduced in 1929 that gave every worker a rest day but no common day off.

The aim was to keep factories running every day, in step with the first Five-Year Plan. The week had five days: four of work and one of rest. Workers were split into groups, each with its own rest day, and the days were marked by colours. Machines never stopped.

It also served the state's campaign against religion, since Sunday disappeared as a shared day of worship. The price was high. Families and friends often had different rest days, so they rarely met. Machines were poorly kept because no one stayed to hand them over.

In 1931 the government changed to a six-day week with a fixed rest day for all. In 1940 the Soviet Union went back to the seven-day week. Stalin's calendar is the sharpest contrast to the weekend of the West, where shared time off became the aim.
sum: The continuous production week, or nepreryvka, was a Soviet work calendar introduced in 1929 that gave every worker a rest day but no common day off.
